title: Reduced training frequencies and maintenance of increased aerobic power
population: Twelve young adults (mean age 23 y) trained 40 min/d, 6 d/wk by cycling and running for 10 weeks, then continued 4 d/wk or 2 d/wk for 15 weeks at unchanged intensity and duration
findings: 10 weeks of training raised VO2max by 25% on cycle tests and 20% on treadmill tests.
VO2max remained essentially at trained levels in both the 4 d/wk and 2 d/wk groups at 5-week checks over 15 weeks of reduced training.
Intensity and duration were unchanged during the reduced-frequency period.
The authors conclude more exercise is needed to increase VO2max than to maintain it, and that VO2max can be maintained for at least 15 weeks with high-intensity training 2 d/wk or 4 d/wk.
limitations: Twelve young adults, two small groups, high-intensity training, 15-week duration; not runners-specific and not distance-endurance or ultra outcomes.
implications: Supports the maintenance-mode finding: 2 sessions per week at unchanged intensity and duration preserved VO2max for 15 weeks in young adults.
Keep intensity and session duration, cut frequency, when only maintenance is needed; treat it as an upper bound of evidence for fitness maintenance, not for injury resilience.
